summary: This unit teaches you how to research business opportunities so that a manager can recommend one with evidence. You will learn to plan the research, choose and test sources, collect your own information ethically, scan the external environment, size a market, check legal and environmental points, compare opportunities with a weighted score and SWOT, and present the findings honestly in a short report.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Business Administration (Management) Level 5 qualification. It is for supervisors and managers who are asked, "Is there a good new business opportunity here?" The answer must not be a hunch. It must be a short, honest report, based on sources you have tested, that shows what is known, what is still uncertain and what should happen next.

Research costs time and money, so it needs a **plan**. You decide what you need to find out, where to look, how much to spend and when to report. You then collect information from published sources (desk research) and from people (field research), analyse it, and compare the opportunities fairly.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means in practice
rows: Plan the research
Agree the aims, scope, budget and deadline; start from the firm's own goals and strengths; write clear research questions.
Find and judge sources
Use official and trade sources, and test every source for who, why, when and how before you trust it.
Collect your own information
Choose surveys, interviews or observation, build a fair sample, and treat people's information properly.
Scan the environment and the market
Use PESTLE, trends, customer needs, competitors, substitutes, seasonality and barriers to entry.
Estimate the size of a market
Work out market size, market share, growth and take-up from the data, and show the working.
Check legal, environmental and ethical points
List licences, standards, registrations and environmental permits and say who to ask.
Compare opportunities
Use SWOT, weighted scoring, opportunity cost and risk to rank the options.
Report the findings
Write a short report that leads with the recommendation, shows the evidence and the sources, and says what is still unknown.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** with scenario and calculation questions (market size, share, growth, weighted scores).
A **written paper** with short answers (exact terms such as qualitative, niche, diaspora, seasonality) and essays.
**Practical group work**: desk research and a research brief with a source log, then customer interviews, a regulatory checklist and a panel briefing.

blocks.note: Practise the market-size sums. Write every step: number of people, percentage, spend, period. Marks go to the working, and a slip in the period (month or year) is the usual error.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Researching without a plan produces a pile of facts and no answer. A manager first asks: **what decision will this research help to make?** Everything else follows from that.

Research should start from the organisation's own **goals and capabilities**: how much it is willing to invest, what it is good at, what it will not do, and what risk it can bear. Ideas found by research must suit the firm. A brilliant opportunity that needs skills, equipment or money the firm cannot get is a poor match, however big the market.

head: Part of the brief
What it says
Example for a Kingston printing firm
rows: Aim
The decision the research supports
Find and rank at least three new services the firm could add
Questions
Specific things to find out
Who would buy? How many? At what price? Who else sells it? What rules apply?
Scope
What is in and what is out
Kingston and St Andrew only; services that use existing printers
Budget
Money and staff time
J$250,000 and one officer for half her time
Deadline
When the findings are due
Report to the board in six weeks
Sources and methods
Where and how to look
Published statistics, trade information, interviews with ten customers

flow: Agree with the sponsor the aims, scope, budget and deadline
Write the research questions, starting from the firm's goals and capabilities
Do the desk research first: it is quicker and cheaper and shows what is still missing
Plan and carry out the field research to fill the gaps
Analyse the findings and compare the opportunities
Report honestly, with a recommendation and a record of sources

blocks.note: Do desk research **before** field research. Published information is quicker and cheaper, it helps you shape better questions for your survey, and it may answer some questions completely.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: A manager who is told what answer the owner wants must still follow the evidence. If the research does not support the idea the managing director favours, report the findings honestly with the evidence.

sections.title: Sources of information and how reliable they are

head: Type
What it is
Examples
Good and bad points
rows: Secondary (desk research)
Information somebody else already collected and published
Official statistics, central bank reports, trade publications, company websites, earlier studies
Quick and cheap. May be out of date or not exactly what you need
Primary (field research)
New information you collect yourself, for your own question
Surveys, interviews, observation, trial sales
Fits your question and is up to date. Costs more time and money

head: Source
What it is useful for
rows: National statistics office (the Statistical Institute of Jamaica, STATIN)
Census and survey figures: population, households by parish, labour force, prices, trade
Planning Institute of Jamaica (PIOJ)
Economic and social reports, national plans and trends
Central bank (Bank of Jamaica)
Exchange rates, interest rates, inflation, economic reports
National investment and export promotion agency (JAMPRO)
Export market information, investment guides, help for exporters
Tourism agencies and the tourist board
Visitor arrivals, cruise calls, visitor spending and trends
Companies Office, the intellectual property office, the tax authority
Business registration, trade mark searches, tax registration
Bureau of Standards and the environment and planning agency
Product standards and labelling; environmental permits and planning
Trade associations, chambers of commerce, trade fairs
Industry news, contacts and views of competitors and buyers
Customers, staff, suppliers
Needs, complaints, prices and gaps that no report shows

blocks.note: Agency names and services change. Check the agency's current website or office for the latest figures and rules, and ask your instructor which sources the Centre uses.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: A source is not reliable just because it looks professional. Ask five questions.

head: Question
What to look for
rows: Who produced it?
Expertise and independence. Official statistics are usually more reliable than an anonymous website.
Why was it produced?
A group that lobbies for a sector, or a firm selling equipment, may show figures in its own favour. Check its figures against an independent source.
How up to date is it?
Fast-changing markets (mobile payments, online sales) need recent data. If you must use an old study, say how old it is and look for newer data.
How was it gathered?
Sample size, who was asked, and whether the method is explained.
Does it agree with other sources?
If three sources give different estimates, compare their methods and use a reasoned range instead of picking the one you like.

blocks.p: Keep a **source log**: for each source, the title, who produced it, the date, what you used it for and your reliability rating with a reason. The log lets others check your findings and update them later, and it protects you if a figure is questioned.

blocks.note: Use public information about rivals, such as their websites, price lists, shop visits and customer reviews. Do not pretend to be someone else to get private information, do not take confidential documents, and do not pay a rival's staff for secrets.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: When published sources do not answer the question, collect your own information. Choose the method that fits the question.

head: Method
Best for
Watch out for
rows: Questionnaire (a set of fixed questions in print or online)
Counting: how many, how often, how much; many people at low cost
Poor questions, a small or unfair sample, low replies
Interview
Understanding why: needs, worries, how people decide; useful when no published data exists
Takes time; the interviewer can influence answers; few people
Focus group
Hearing a group discuss an idea or product
A strong voice can dominate
Observation
What people really do, such as traffic in a shop or queues at a stall
Cannot tell why people act as they do
Trial or pilot
What people really buy and pay
Needs a product and some money to run

blocks.p: **Quantitative** research gives numbers (for example, 40% would use the service). **Qualitative** research gives words and reasons, such as opinions from interviews. Good research usually uses both: interviews to find what matters, then a questionnaire to measure how many people feel that way.

ul: Use **open questions** to explore needs: "What makes it hard to get your medicine?" Use **closed questions** to count: "Would you pay J$500 a month? Yes or no."
Avoid **leading questions** that suggest the answer: "Wouldn't you agree that delivery is a great idea?"
Ask one thing at a time, in plain words, and test the questionnaire on a few people first.
Include price questions, but remember that what people say they will pay is only a guide. The best test is to ask target customers to react to a real price.

blocks.p: You cannot ask everyone, so you ask a **sample**. The sample must represent the group you want to know about. A survey of people at one shopping mall on a weekday morning misses shift workers and people who do not go to that mall. The result will not describe the target market.

ul: Define the target group first, such as "small guest houses in a parish".
Ask a mix of people: different ages, places, times and, where relevant, income levels.
Check how many replies you need, for example 10% of 3,500 taxi operators is 350.
Record how the sample was chosen so readers can judge it.

blocks.note: In a survey, 40% of people saying they "would probably buy" does **not** mean 40% will buy. People overstate. Treat it as a rough, upper-end guide to demand and test with real buying where you can.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: Tell people why you are asking, and that they may refuse.
Get **consent** before you keep their contact details or use them for another purpose, such as a later sales call. State the purpose.
Store the details safely and keep only what you need, in line with the data protection law.
Record interview answers without names if you promised that.
Do not share a list of people's details with another firm unless they agreed.

sections.title: Scanning the environment and the market

blocks.p: PESTLE helps you scan the outside world in an organised way, so no factor is missed. Record each finding under one heading and say how it affects the opportunity.

head: Factor
What to research
Example finding and what it means
rows: Political
Government policy, incentives, trade agreements
A new incentive for agro-processing: lower cost for a processor
Economic
Incomes, exchange rate, interest rates, energy costs
Rising electricity prices: higher cost for a business that uses ovens or fryers
Social
Population, age, lifestyle, tastes
The population of a town is ageing: more demand for home care and mobility aids
Technological
New equipment, online tools, mobile payments
More shops accept card payments: demand for card readers
Legal
Licences, standards, labelling, employment and data rules
A new rule requires all food vendors to be certified: demand for training; a barrier for new vendors
Environmental
Weather, floods, drought, waste and water rules
Flooding cuts crop supply: risk for a processor; demand for flood-proof storage

blocks.p: A trend is a change over time, such as more phones in use and kept for longer. A **gap** is a need that nobody meets well. For example, if research in a town finds many working parents but no after-school care centre within 10 km, that suggests a possible gap worth studying further. A gap is a lead, not proof: check that enough customers want it and will pay.

Find out who the possible customers are, their **needs, habits and price limits**, where they buy now, and what they complain about. Describe a **target market** and look for a **niche**: a small, specialised part of a market that larger firms tend to ignore.

Some markets are overseas. The **diaspora** (Jamaicans and people of Jamaican descent living abroad) is often researched as a market for Jamaican food, products and services. Research should then include the import rules, food standards, shipping costs and labelling of the destination country.

head: Type
Meaning
What to find out
rows: Direct competitor
Sells the same thing to the same customers
Prices, range, location, hours, how it reaches customers, apparent size, years trading, reviews
Indirect competitor or substitute
Meets the same need in a different way (a bus ride instead of a taxi)
How many customers it takes and why they choose it

blocks.p: Look for signs of change, such as a rival expanding or closing, and for patterns. If three car-wash businesses in a town are busy at weekends and quiet on weekdays, there may be room for a weekday offer to fleets and companies. Study also the **barriers to entry**, the things that make it hard for a new firm to start, such as costly licences and equipment, a need for specialist skills or strong customer loyalty to existing firms.

ul: **Suppliers:** check that the inputs are available, steady and affordable. A bottled-sauce opportunity depends on peppers, bottles and labels.

**Seasonality:** regular rises and falls at the same times each year. Beach and tourism businesses may have strong winter sales and a quiet September and October, so cash and staffing must allow for the quiet months.
**Dependence on one customer:** two opportunities with similar profit are not equal if one depends on a single large customer, which adds risk.

blocks.note: Porter's five forces (rivals, new entrants, substitutes, buyers, suppliers) is a useful check on how attractive an industry is. Use it with PESTLE: PESTLE looks at the wider environment, five forces looks at the industry.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Estimating the size of a market

blocks.p: Managers need numbers: how big is the market, how much could we win, and is it growing? The calculations are simple, but mistakes with percentages and periods are common. Always show the working and check it twice.

head: Measure
Formula
What it tells you
rows: Market size (a year)
People or households × percentage who would buy × spend per period × number of periods
The total spending available, not your firm's sales
Market share
Firm's sales ÷ total market × 100
The slice of the market a firm has or aims for
Sales target from share
Market size × target share
The sales a firm would earn at that share
Growth rate
(New − old) ÷ old × 100
How fast a market or a number is rising or falling
Take-up rate
Number who use ÷ number asked or eligible × 100
How many of the target group actually use the product
Average spend
Total spending ÷ number of customers
What a typical customer spends

blocks.h: Worked example: market size and share

blocks.p: A town has 12,000 households. Research suggests 30% would buy a water-filter service and each would spend J$3,000 a month.

ol: A new firm that aims for a 3% share: 129,600,000 × 3% = **J$3,888,000** a year.

blocks.p: Check: 3% of 3,600 households is 108 households; 108 × 3,000 × 12 = 3,888,000.

blocks.h: Worked example: growth, take-up and average spend

ul: A market grew from J$120 million to J$138 million. Growth = (138 − 120) ÷ 120 = 18 ÷ 120 = **15%**.
A survey of 1,500 small shops finds that 450 use an online stock system. Take-up = 450 ÷ 1,500 = **30%**.
200 customers spent J$800,000 in total at a rival. Average spend = 800,000 ÷ 200 = **J$4,000**.

blocks.note: The **percentage increase** divides by the **old** figure, not the new one. A rise from 80 to 100 is 20 ÷ 80 = 25%, not 20%.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: The market size is the **total** spend. The firm's sales will be only a part of it, because existing taxis, shops or competitors will keep a share.
Percentages taken from surveys are often **stated intentions**, which overstate real buying.
Price, student or household numbers and rules can change. Give a **range** (for example, low, expected and high cases) and say what the estimate depends on.
Improve it by checking numbers with an official source, testing the price with target customers and doing a small trial.

blocks.p: An opportunity that is illegal, or that needs permits you cannot get, is not an opportunity. The research must list the points to check and say which agency to ask. Refer to the law by its purpose and confirm details with the agency or a qualified adviser; a manager does not memorise every rule.

head: Opportunity
Legal and regulatory points to research
rows: Preparing and selling food
Licences and permits, food safety approvals and inspections, labelling rules
Carrying passengers or running tours for visitors
Licences to carry passengers for hire, vehicle and driver requirements, insurance, rules for tour guides and operators
Exporting a food product
Rules and food standards of the importing country, labelling, packaging, shipping documents and export support
Making goods under a brand name
Whether the name is already a trade mark; registering your own; protecting designs and recipes
Opening a quarry, a plant or a farm business
Environmental permits and planning approval; effects on land and water; waste
Employing staff
Employment law (contracts, pay, hours, safe working conditions) and statutory deductions
Collecting customers' details
The data protection law: consent, purpose, safe storage
Any new business
Registration under company law or as a business name, tax registration including GCT where it applies

blocks.p: When the opportunity is to buy an existing business or to join a partner, research must include **due diligence**: careful checking of the facts, finances and legal position before committing. This covers the accounts, debts, contracts, the lease, licences and any disputes.

blocks.note: If the team cannot answer tax or company-law questions, tell the manager to seek advice from a qualified adviser, such as an accountant or an attorney-at-law. Say so in the report instead of guessing.
blocks.label: Tip

ul: Report findings honestly, including those that do not support the idea the director favours.
Do not use dishonest methods to get information about rivals.
Protect research respondents' personal details.
Make clear which figures are facts, which are estimates and which are opinions.

sections.title: Comparing opportunities and reaching a recommendation

blocks.p: PESTLE shows the outside factors. A **SWOT** adds the firm's own view: strengths and weaknesses (inside) and opportunities and threats (outside). Use both: an opportunity such as strong demand for solar panel installation still raises the internal question, "Do we have, or can we get, the skills?"

flow: Agree the criteria that matter most to the firm: demand, profit, start-up cost, fit with skills, risk
Give each criterion a weight; the weights must add up to 100%
Score each opportunity on each criterion, for example out of 10, using the research findings
Multiply each score by its weight and add the results
Rank the opportunities and test the result by changing a weight or a score

head: Criterion
Weight
P score
P weighted
Q score
Q weighted
rows: Demand
Profit
Fit with skills
**Total**

blocks.p: Q scores 7.3 against 7.2, so the options are almost level. A margin that small tells the team to look for more evidence on the two or three scores that matter most, not to declare a winner. The strengths of weighted scoring are that it makes the team agree what matters, is easy to explain to a board and uses the research in a structured way. The weakness is that the scores and weights are still judgements, which can be pushed to fit a favourite.

If resources allow only one opportunity, the **opportunity cost** of choosing one is the benefit given up from the idea not chosen. Report also the main risks: dependence on one customer, seasonality, imported inputs and rules that may change.

A **feasibility study** tests whether an idea can work, in more depth than the first research: technical, market, legal, financial and operational. The usual next step after research shows strong demand, a good fit and manageable risks is to recommend a full feasibility study or a business plan, not to start spending on the venture. If the research is weak, recommend more research or dropping the idea, and say why.

blocks.note: A recommendation can be "do not proceed". An honest negative finding saves the firm money and is a successful piece of research.
blocks.label: Remember

sections.title: Reporting and building research into the routine

blocks.p: A busy board reads the first page. Put the answer there.

head: Section
What it does
rows: Summary (one page)
The purpose, the opportunities found, the main findings and the recommendation
Introduction
Aims, scope and limits agreed at the start
Methods and sources
The desk and field research done, the sources used and their reliability, so the reader can judge the evidence
Findings
For each opportunity: market size and trends, customers, competitors, legal points, resources needed, main risks, in tables and charts
Comparison
The weighted score or other comparison, with the reasoning
Conclusions and recommendation
What is known, what is uncertain, and what to do next
Appendices
Questionnaire, interview notes (without names), the source log, detailed tables

ul: Use plain words, short paragraphs and numbered tables.
Show the working for any calculation.
Separate facts, estimates and opinions.
Name the limits: "The survey covered 120 people in one town."

blocks.p: Opportunities appear all year, so research should be a habit, not a one-off. A simple scanning system names who watches which sources: official statistics and central bank reports for economic trends, government announcements for incentives and rules, trade publications and fairs for products and technology, customer complaints and requests for unmet needs. Sales staff and drivers record ideas in a shared log. Once a month the management team reviews the log, looks for patterns and chooses one or two ideas to research further. Once a year, a fuller PESTLE and SWOT review feeds into planning. Ideas are screened with agreed criteria so time is not wasted.

Trade fairs and business associations help by offering contacts and market news. The benefit of a routine is that the firm sees changes earlier than rivals and spends research money only on ideas that pass a first screen.

ul: write a research brief with aims, questions, scope, budget, deadline and sources.
start the research from the firm's own goals and capabilities.
tell desk research from field research and primary from secondary information.
test a source for who, why, when, how and agreement with others, and keep a source log.
choose between questionnaires, interviews, observation and trials, and write open and closed questions.
build a fair sample and explain why a biased sample misleads.
treat respondents' information with consent and care.
use PESTLE, trends, customer needs, competitor information, substitutes, seasonality and barriers to entry.
calculate market size, share, growth, take-up and average spend, with the working shown.
list the legal, environmental and ethical points to check and say who to ask.
compare opportunities with weighted scoring, SWOT, opportunity cost and risk.
write a short report with the recommendation first and the limits of the evidence stated.

terms: Research using information already published, done at a desk.
Collecting new information directly from people or places.
New information collected by the researcher.
Information already collected and published by someone else.
Data in words, such as opinions from interviews.
A set of fixed questions used to collect answers in a survey.
The part of a group that is asked, chosen to represent the whole.
A record of every source used, with its date and a reliability rating.
A small, specialised part of a market that larger firms tend to ignore.
Jamaicans and people of Jamaican descent living overseas.
A different product that meets the same customer need.
Something that makes it hard for a new firm to enter a market.
Regular rises and falls in demand at the same times each year.
A firm's sales as a percentage of the total market.
The share of the target group that actually uses a product.
Scores multiplied by the importance weights of each criterion and added up.
The benefit given up from the option not chosen.
Careful checking of the facts, finances and legal position before committing.
A test of whether an idea can work.

c1.title: Frozen Jamaican meals for the United Kingdom
c1.text: Nadine Powell is an officer at a Kingston catering firm. The managing director asks her to research selling frozen Jamaican meals to Jamaicans in the United Kingdom. She has six weeks and J$400,000. Her first finds are an online guide written by a shipping agent who sells freight to the UK, which says that demand for Jamaican food there is "booming", and a UK government census table.

c2.title: Drip-irrigation kits in Santa Cruz
c2.text: A farm-supplies shop in Santa Cruz, St Elizabeth, is studying the market for drip-irrigation kits in the parish. Official figures show 8,000 farm households. A survey at a farmers' fair suggests 20% would buy a kit, spending about J$45,000 each. The shop wants a 5% share of the market. Last year it sold 1,200 kits of all types; this year it sold 1,500.

c3.title: Home delivery for a Spanish Town pharmacy
c3.text: A community pharmacy in Spanish Town has 2,400 registered patients and is thinking of offering home delivery. The pharmacist asks her assistant to run a survey. The assistant hands out forms to people who come to the counter on a Saturday morning. 120 forms are returned, and 30 say they would use delivery. The pharmacist also wants to pass the patients' phone numbers to a courier firm so that it can test the idea.

c4.title: Choosing between three jobs for a Mandeville workshop
c4.text: An engineering workshop in Mandeville can follow only one new line of work. It scored three options on demand (weight 35%), profit (30%), fit with skills (25%) and low risk (10%, where a higher score means safer). A, metal furniture for hotels, scored 8, 6, 9 and 5. B, repair work for one large farm co-operative, scored 6, 9, 7 and 3. C, gates for housing developments, scored 7, 7, 6 and 9.

c5.title: A banana-chip processor in St Mary
c5.text: A small firm in St Mary makes banana chips. It is researching a larger factory. The research team has noted: a new rule on food labelling; rising electricity costs for the fryers; growing interest in healthy snacks; heavy flooding that cut the supply of bananas last year; and a government incentive for agro-processing. The manager has also asked the team to find out about two rival producers.

questions.q: Which is the best statement of Nadine's research aim?
o: Prove to the managing director that the idea is a good one
Size the UK market and find the import rules
Collect as many views about Jamaican food as she can
Find out everything about the UK food market
questions.why: A good aim supports a decision and fits the scope, time and money: the market size and the rules. Research that tries to prove an idea, or to cover everything, produces bias or waste.

questions.q: How should Nadine treat the shipping agent's guide that says demand is "booming"?
o: Accept it, because a shipping agent knows the UK trade well
Ignore it completely, because it was published online
Quote it in the report as the main evidence of demand
Use it as a lead and check it against another source
questions.why: The agent profits from more freight, so the figures may be shown in its favour. A source with an interest is checked against an independent one before it is relied on.

questions.q: Which is the best source for the number of people of Jamaican origin in the UK?
o: The UK government census tables
A poll in a social media group for Jamaicans abroad
An advert by a Jamaican restaurant in London
A friend's estimate from living in the UK
questions.why: Official census tables are produced by an independent public body with a clear method. An online poll, an advert or a guess is unrepresentative or interested.

questions.q: Nadine reads the census table and published reports. What type of research is this?
o: Field research using primary information
Qualitative research using interviews
Desk research using published data
Observation of customers in shops
questions.why: Information that someone else collected and published is secondary, and reading it at a desk is desk research. Do it first, because it is quicker and cheaper than field research.

questions.q: What is the estimated yearly market for kits in the parish?
If the shop wins its target 5% share, what are its yearly kit sales?
questions.why: Sales at a given share = market size × share = 72,000,000 × 0.05 = J$3,600,000. Check: 80 of the 1,600 households × J$45,000 = J$3,600,000.

questions.q: By what percentage did the shop's yearly kit sales rise?
questions.why: Growth = (new − old) ÷ old = (1,500 − 1,200) ÷ 1,200 = 300 ÷ 1,200 = 25%. Dividing by the new figure gives 20%, which is the usual mistake.

questions.q: The 20% buying figure came from a survey at a farmers' fair. What is the best way to use it?
o: As a firm forecast, since the farmers said it themselves
As an upper-end guide, because fewer will really buy
As proof of demand, because the fair was well attended
As unusable, because a survey cannot show demand
questions.why: Stated intentions overstate real buying, and fair visitors are probably keener than the average farmer. Use it as a rough upper limit, show a range, and test with a trial or pre-orders.

questions.q: What is the main weakness of the assistant's survey method?
o: The forms were handed out only on a Saturday morning
It misses housebound patients who cannot come in
Only 120 of the 2,400 patients were asked to reply
Paper forms were used instead of an online survey
questions.why: Delivery would help most the people who find it hard to come in, and the survey cannot reach them. The sample does not represent the target market. The sample size is a smaller concern.

questions.q: What is the take-up rate among those who returned forms?
questions.why: Take-up = 30 ÷ 120 × 100 = 25%. Check: 25% of 120 = 30. It describes only the 120 who answered, not all 2,400 patients.

questions.q: What should the pharmacist do about passing the phone numbers to the courier firm?
o: Not pass them on unless the patients consent
Pass them on, since the patients are registered customers
Pass them on if the courier promises to keep them private
Pass them on after removing the patients' surnames
questions.why: Personal details collected for one purpose should not be shared for another without consent. The data protection law expects consent, a stated purpose and safe handling.

questions.q: Which question is best for a follow-up interview with an older patient?
o: Wouldn't you agree that home delivery is a great idea?
Do you want delivery? Please answer yes or no.
How much would you pay for delivery each month?
What makes it hard for you to get your medicine?
questions.why: An open question about the problem invites the patient's own words and reasons. A leading question suggests the answer, and a closed question gives no reasons.

questions.q: Which option has the highest weighted score?
o: C, gates for housing developments, with 6.95
B, repairs for the co-operative, with 6.85
A, metal furniture for hotels, with 6.95
A, metal furniture for hotels, with 7.35

questions.q: What is option B's weighted score?
If the workshop chooses A, what is the opportunity cost?
o: The money it has already spent on researching all three
The cost of the metal and labour for the furniture
The benefit it gives up from the next best option, C
The profit it expects to earn from the furniture
questions.why: Opportunity cost is the benefit given up by not choosing the next best alternative. Money already spent is a sunk cost, and the furniture's own costs and profit belong to the option chosen.

questions.q: The owner says fit with skills should count for more than 25%. What is the best response?
o: Re-score with the new weights and compare rankings
Change the scores of option A so that it still wins
Drop the matrix and choose by the owner's preference
Leave the weights as they are, because they were agreed first
questions.why: Testing how sensitive the result is to a change of weight shows how firm the ranking is. Changing scores to protect a favourite, or ignoring the matrix, defeats the purpose of using one.

questions.q: Under PESTLE, where does the new labelling rule go?
o: Legal
Political
Economic
Social
questions.why: A rule on food labelling is a legal factor. The research must show what the firm has to change and what it will cost. The incentive belongs under Political.

questions.q: Rising electricity costs for the fryers belong under which PESTLE heading?
o: Environmental
Technological
Social
Economic
questions.why: Energy costs are an economic factor that affects the cost of making each bag of chips. Flooding is environmental and healthy-snack interest is social.

questions.q: Which method is ethical for finding out about the two rival producers?
o: Asking a friend who works there to copy their customer list
Reading their websites and public customer reviews
Pretending to be a buyer to get a private price quotation
Offering a rival's driver money for its supplier details
questions.why: Public information such as websites, labels and public reviews is fair to use. Copying lists, deceiving a rival or paying for secrets is unethical and may be unlawful.

questions.q: A researcher needs replies from 6% of the 2,500 members of a farmers' co-operative. How many replies is that?
questions.why: 6% of 2,500 = 0.06 × 2,500 = 150. Check: 150 ÷ 2,500 = 0.06. Treating 6% as 0.6 gives 15, a common slip.
